issues.legal_issue: A court must independently determine that the price offered for a company’s property in liquidation is adequate before confirming a sale that is subject to its confirmation.
material_facts: The sale was of a company’s assets in liquidation, and acceptance of an offer by the commissioners was subject to confirmation by the court.
The agreed advertising requirements were not fully followed, the initial process attracted only one offer, and the court received higher offers after the sale process had begun.
The court had information indicating that the property might be worth more than the accepted offer.
issues.conclusion: The initial offer should not have been confirmed without the court being satisfied that the price was adequate; in the circumstances, the sale required a fresh process.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, sales may be conducted by public auction, sealed tenders, or another manner directed by the Judge. Confirmation is a safeguard against an inadequate sale price, and the court must exercise its discretion judicially, having regard to the interests of the company and its creditors. The Court relied on Gordhan Das Chuni Lal v. T. Sriman Kanthimathinatha Pillai, AIR 1921 Mad 286; Rathnaswami Pillai v. Sadapathi Pillai, AIR 1925 Mad 318; S. Soundarajan v. M/s. Roshan & Co., AIR 1951 Mad 986; and A. Subbaraya Mudaliar v. K. Sundarajan, cited in the judgment as AIR 1951 Mad 1986.

predicates.company_property_sale_in_liquidation: A company’s property is being sold as part of its liquidation.
predicates.court_confirmation_required: The terms of the sale make the court’s confirmation a condition of the sale.
predicates.offered_price_not_reasonable: The circumstances relied on by the court show that the offered price is not reasonable having regard to the property’s market value.

issues.definition: When a sale of a company’s property in liquidation requires court confirmation and the offered price is not reasonable, confirmation must be refused.

issues.legal_issue: A sale process cannot be treated as a public auction when inadequate notice or restrictions prevent the public from having a fair opportunity to participate.
material_facts: The sale proclamation was not advertised in all the required newspapers or with the required frequency.
After receiving higher offers, the Judge held an immediate auction confined to the original offeror and one other offeror.
The auction was not announced to the public, and other potential purchasers had no opportunity to participate.
issues.conclusion: The restricted, inadequately publicized auction was not a public sale and did not provide a sound basis for confirming the bid; a fresh sale by sealed tenders or public auction was required.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, permits sale by public auction, sealed tenders, or another manner directed by the Judge. A public sale entails notice to the public and liberty for members of the public to participate. Lack of publicity and opportunity to bid may cause inherent prejudice to the company and its creditors and invalidate confirmation.

rule.if: company_property_sale_in_liquidation and public_notice_inadequate and auction_restricted_to_selected_bidders and public_participation_denied

predicates.company_property_sale_in_liquidation: A company’s property is being sold as part of its liquidation.
predicates.public_notice_inadequate: The sale was not publicized sufficiently to give potential purchasers fair notice.
predicates.auction_restricted_to_selected_bidders: The auction was confined to persons selected or already involved in the sale process.
predicates.public_participation_denied: Members of the public who might have bid were not given an opportunity to participate.

issues.definition: When a company’s property is being sold in liquidation without adequate public notice and the auction is restricted so that the public cannot participate, a fresh sale must be ordered.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may interfere with a judge’s discretionary confirmation of a sale when the judge has departed from the governing principles for conducting the sale.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the confirmation of a sale of company property in liquidation.
The Judge chose to hold an auction but confined it to two persons and did not provide prior public notice.
The resulting process denied other potential purchasers an opportunity to bid and risked prejudice to the company and its creditors.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was right to set aside the confirmation and direct a fresh sale because the Judge went wrong in principle by not holding a duly publicized public auction.
issues.legal_principle: A discretionary decision should not ordinarily be disturbed unless the judge has gone wrong on principle. The Court applied that standard alongside Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, and the requirement that a public auction provide notice to the public and an opportunity to participate.

predicates.appeal_from_sale_confirmation: An appeal challenges a court’s confirmation of a sale.
predicates.lower_court_exercised_discretion: The lower court made a discretionary decision about whether to confirm the sale.
predicates.lower_court_departed_from_sale_principle: The lower court conducted or confirmed the sale in a manner inconsistent with the principles governing a fair and public sale.

issues.definition: On an appeal from sale confirmation, appellate interference is justified when the lower court exercised discretion but departed from the principles governing the sale.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent higher offer alone does not justify refusing confirmation once the court is satisfied that the sale price is adequate.
material_facts: A later offeror proposed a higher price after the commissioners had accepted the original offer.
Another higher offer was made before confirmation, with a complaint that inadequate publicity had prevented a timely offer.
The Court held that the sale process in this case did not establish an adequate price because publicity and public participation had been inadequate.
issues.conclusion: A higher subsequent offer cannot by itself justify refusing confirmation if the court has already concluded that the offered price is adequate; that condition was not met in this case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that once the court concludes that the price offered is adequate, no subsequent higher offer is a valid ground for refusing confirmation of the sale or offer already received. It relied on S. Soundarajan v. M/s. Roshan & Co., AIR 1951 Mad 986, while also applying the court’s duty to assess adequacy before confirmation.

predicates.company_property_sale_in_liquidation: A company’s property is being sold as part of its liquidation.
predicates.court_finds_price_adequate: The court has concluded that the offered price is adequate having regard to the property’s market value.
predicates.subsequent_higher_offer_made: A person makes a higher offer after the offer under consideration has been received or accepted.

issues.definition: When the court finds the price adequate in a company liquidation sale, a subsequent higher offer alone does not justify refusing confirmation.
